title: Data Standards
text:
Data Standards
This page serves as a reference for the metadata terms used by the Reef Archive to describe historical coral reef photographs. Each term lists its definition, examples, is marked as required or optional, and where relevant, the EXIF tag it maps to in the media file.
The terms are adapted from the Darwin Core standard and the Camera Trap Data Package (CamTrap DP), so that Reef Archive data can be shared with, and understood by, the wider biodiversity data community. Where a term follows Darwin Core or CamTrap DP, its meaning is equivalent; where the Reef Archive has added or modified a term, the definition on this page is the one that applies.
Need help? If something here is unclear, or you are unsure how to describe a media file, get in touch at info@reefarchive.org or open an issue on the Reef Archive GitHub repository.
Want to contribute? Suggestions for new terms, or changes to existing definitions and examples, are welcome. Please propose them as an issue or pull request on the GitHub repository.
How do I cite this? Archived media and metadata are deposited in the Reef Archive community on Zenodo. Please cite the relevant record, and the bibliographicCitation and license given for each media file, when reusing images or data.


List of Terms

mediaIDRequiredDefinitionA unique identifier for the media file. Concatenating collectionID and fileName is considered best practice.Examples10.5281/zenodo.22663465-IMG0001EXIF tagImageUniqueID
fileNameRequiredDefinitionThe name of the media file. Prefixing still images with "IMG" and and moving images with "MOV" is considered best practice.ExamplesIMG0001, MOV0001EXIF tagOriginalRawFileName
collectionIDRequiredDefinitionA unique identifier for the collection. Using a stable Digital Object Identifier is considered best practice. Examples10.5281/zenodo.22663465
collectionNameRequiredDefinitionThe name of the collection.ExamplesEileen Graham's Collection, Discovery Bay, Jamaica, (1966–1968).EXIF tagImageDescription
typeRequiredDefinitionThe nature of the resource. Constraints: StillImage, MovingImage.ExamplesStillImage, MovingImage
bibliographicCitationRequiredDefinitionA bibliographic reference for the resource.ExamplesJohnson, K. and Jones, L.A. (2026) Eileen Graham Collection, Discovery Bay, Jamaica (1966–1968). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22663465.
licenseRequiredDefinitionA legal document giving official permission to do something with the resource.Exampleshttp://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcodeEXIF tagCopyright
rightsHolderRequiredDefinitionA person or organisation owning or managing rights over the resource.ExamplesTrustees of the Natural History MuseumEXIF tagCopyright
capturedByRequiredDefinitionName or identifier of the person or organisation that captured the media.ExamplesEileen GrahamEXIF tagArtist
digitisedByRequiredDefinitionName or identifier of the person or organisation that digitised the media.ExamplesKenneth Johnson
processedByRequiredDefinitionName or identifier of the person or organisation that processed the media.ExamplesLewis A. Jones
yearRequiredDefinitionThe four-digit year in which the media was captured, according to the Common Era Calendar.Examples1984EXIF tagDateTimeOriginal
monthOptionalDefinitionThe integer month in which the media was captured.Examples6EXIF tagDateTimeOriginal
dayOptionalDefinitionThe integer day of the month in which the media was captured.Examples3EXIF tagDateTimeOriginal
habitatOptionalDefinitionA category or description of the habitat in which the media was captured.Examplesreef flat, reef edge, reef slopeEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
waterBodyOptionalDefinitionThe name of the water body in which the media was captured.ExamplesThe Caribbean SeaEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
islandGroupOptionalDefinitionThe name of the island group in which the media was captured.ExamplesGreater AntillesEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
islandOptionalDefinitionThe name of the island in which the media was captured.ExamplesJamaicaEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
countryOptionalDefinitionThe name of the country or major administrative unit in which the media was captured.ExamplesJamaicaEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
countryCodeOptionalDefinitionThe standard code for the country in which the media was captured (ISO 3166-1-alpha-2).ExamplesJMEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
stateProvinceOptionalDefinitionThe name of the next smaller administrative region than country (state, province, canton, department, region, etc.) in which the media was captured.EXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
countyOptionalDefinitionThe full, unabbreviated name of the next smaller administrative region than stateProvince (county, shire, department, etc.) in which the media was captured.ExamplesSaint Ann Parish, Middlesex CountyEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
municipalityOptionalDefinitionThe full, unabbreviated name of the next smaller administrative region than county (city, municipality, etc.) in which the media was captured.ExamplesDiscovery BayEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
localityOptionalDefinitionThe specific description of the place.ExamplesPinnacle 1 Sand SlopeEXIF tagGPSAreaInformation
decimalLongitudeRequiredDefinitionA geographic longitude (in decimal degrees) as per EPSG:4326 geodetic datum.Examples-121.1761111EXIF tagGPSLongitude
decimalLatitudeRequiredDefinitionA geographic latitude (in decimal degrees) as per EPSG:4326 geodetic datum.Examples-41.0983423EXIF tagGPSLatitude
georeferenceRemarksOptionalDefinitionComments or notes about the spatial description determination, explaining assumptions made or the protocol.ExamplesCoordinates inferred from local feature (buoy), precise to the nearest minute (0.01).EXIF tagUserComment
minimumDepthInMetresOptionalDefinitionThe least depth within a range of depths in metres.Examples10EXIF tagWaterDepth
maximumDepthInMetresOptionalDefinitionThe greatest depth within a range of depths in metres.Examples25EXIF tagWaterDepth
mediaCommentsOptionalDefinitionAny comments or notes about the media file.ExamplesMedia file corrupted.EXIF tagUserComment
modifiedRequiredDefinitionDate on which the resource was changed. Formatted as an ISO 8601 string (YYYY-MM-DD).Examples1969-02-12

title: Contribute
text:
Contribute
Reef Archive is an open repository of historical coral reef imagery, and anyone, anywhere in the world, is welcome to contribute. If you have reef images from pre-1990s (slides, prints, negatives or scans), we would love to hear from you.


Become an early contributor
Reef Archive is currently in a pilot phase and is operating without dedicated funding, which limits our infrastructure and capacity. We are seeking support for the project’s long-term sustainability, and the strongest case we can make to funders is a collection that shows what the archive can be. Early contributors are central to that: every image donated now helps demonstrate the value of the project.


How to contribute
Our long-term goal is to develop semi-automated workflows for ingesting historical imagery. Until then, we work with contributors directly. To get started, email info@reefarchive.org and we will guide you through the process. We can help with every step, which is roughly:

Digitise analogue images (slides, prints and negatives).
Prepare and link metadata such as who took the photograph, where and when.
Review and conform the metadata to our data standard.
Archive the images on Zenodo and add them to the Reef Archive website.

You don’t need to have everything ready, and even partial information about an image is useful. Just get in touch.


Other ways to help
If you don’t have images to contribute but would like to support the project, whether through funding, collaboration or spreading the word, please get in touch.

title: About The Reef Archive
text:
About The Reef Archive
Coral reefs have changed profoundly over the past half-century: bleached, eroded, and diminished in ways that are now so familiar they risk becoming the new normal. Yet scattered across attics, filing cabinets, and forgotten hard drives lies a remarkable counter-record: thousands of underwater photographs taken by pioneering reef scientists in the 1950s through to the 1990s, documenting reefs as they once were.
These images are primary scientific evidence. They offer site-specific, empirical glimpses of reef communities before the widespread declines of the 1980s and before long-term monitoring programmes existed to capture them. They show what “healthy” actually looked like — the benthic assemblages, coral cover, and structural complexity that managers and policy makers now struggle to define without a reliable baseline. Without such baselines, conservation targets risk being anchored to an already-degraded present.
But this record is disappearing. Ageing film degrades. Scientists retire or pass away. Institutional memory fades. These archives — invaluable precisely because they are irreplaceable — have no natural home, and so they are quietly being lost.
The Reef Archive exists to change that.
We are building an open-access, community-curated repository for legacy reef imagery and its associated metadata (precise locations, dates, depths, photographers, and ecological context) hosted both here and on Zenodo. Our goal is to rescue this visual record, make it freely accessible to researchers, conservationists, and the public, and preserve it for the generations of scientists who will need it most.
